title: How do you generate globally-unique IDs across shards: a DB sequence per shard with non-overlapping ranges, a Snowflake-style ID generator (timestamp + worker-id + sequence), or UUIDv7?
keyPoints: Globally-unique IDs across shards must never collide even though many independent nodes create them in parallel, without a central bottleneck.
Per-shard sequences with non-overlapping ranges use interleaving (increment by N, start at offset k) or range blocks for simple, compact integer IDs.
Snowflake-style IDs pack a timestamp, worker ID, and per-millisecond sequence into a 64-bit integer, giving time-sorted uniqueness with no coordination.
UUIDv7 is a 128-bit ID with a millisecond timestamp prefix, providing collision-resistant uniqueness with zero coordination and time-ordered inserts.
Avoid random UUIDv4 as a primary key on large tables because random inserts fragment B-trees and thrash the buffer cache.
Time-ordered IDs (Snowflake, UUIDv7) keep inserts append-friendly, maintaining good index locality.
The shard key and ID strategy should be decided together since the ID often determines which shard a row belongs to.

s1_definition.oneliner: Make IDs globally unique without a central bottleneck using per-shard non-overlapping sequence ranges, a Snowflake-style timestamp-plus-worker-plus-counter 64-bit id, or time-ordered UUIDv7.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Per-shard sequences** – Each shard has a database sequence configured with non-overlapping ranges, either interleaved (increment by N, offset k) or block-allocated.
- **Snowflake-style** – A 64-bit integer packing a timestamp in the high bits, a worker/machine ID, and a per-millisecond sequence counter.
- **UUIDv7** – A 128-bit UUID with a millisecond timestamp prefix and random suffix, giving time-ordered uniqueness with zero coordination.
- **Key principle** – Avoid random UUIDv4 on large tables because random inserts fragment the B-tree and thrash the cache.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India has many branches (shards) issuing account reference numbers at the same time, and two branches must never issue the same number. One way is to give each branch a different number block so they can never clash. Another is a smart stamp combining the current time, the branch ID, and a counter, guaranteeing uniqueness without phoning head office. A third is a very long random-but-time-sorted code (UUIDv7) that is practically impossible to duplicate and still sorts by creation time.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Generating globally-unique IDs across shards means letting many independent nodes mint identifiers in parallel that never collide, without funneling every insert through a central ID server. The three strategies trade off differently. Per-shard sequences with interleaved ranges give compact integer IDs and need no coordination at insert time, but adding shards requires reconfiguring sequences. Snowflake-style IDs pack a timestamp, worker ID, and per-millisecond sequence into a compact 64-bit integer, giving time-sorted uniqueness with no network call, but require worker ID assignment and clock skew handling. UUIDv7 provides zero-coordination 128-bit IDs with a timestamp prefix, at the cost of larger keys and more storage.

The critical rule is to avoid random UUIDv4 as a primary key on large tables. Random inserts scatter across the B-tree, causing page splits, fragmentation, and poor cache locality. Time-ordered IDs (Snowflake, UUIDv7) keep inserts near the end of the index, maintaining append-friendly behavior.

At the National Bank of India, sharded transactions needed unique IDs minted concurrently. Rajesh used per-shard interleaved sequences for compact integer transaction IDs, and for a high-throughput event stream across many nodes, the team used Snowflake IDs because a compact, time-sortable 64-bit ID mattered for index locality.

Remember one sentence: make IDs globally unique without a central bottleneck using per-shard non-overlapping sequences, a Snowflake-style timestamp-plus-worker-plus-counter, or time-ordered UUIDv7.
